sourceTitle: Asteroids: A Question of Risk, Not Panic
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original astronomy assessment variant; factual, CEFR and pedagogical review pending.

questions.q: Why can the phrase 'heading towards Earth' be misleading in a headline?
choices: Any asteroid moving towards Earth must be made of metal.
It can sound like a collision prediction without enough orbital evidence.
It shows that scientists have already ruled out every possible risk.
It describes only objects that are invisible to telescopes.
questions.explanation: The opening distinguishes a close approach from a path that would actually intersect Earth.

questions.q: Why does the writer challenge the everyday meaning of the word 'near'?
choices: It is a term used only for spacecraft close to the Moon.
It usually refers to distance below one hundred kilometres.
It cannot be calculated without infrared observations.
Distances described as near in space can still be enormous.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one warns that cosmic proximity is not the same as everyday closeness.

questions.q: What is the value of comparing observations from several nights?
choices: It proves every early impact prediction must be wrong.
It allows telescopes to see only the brightest objects.
It refines the asteroid's orbit as more evidence becomes available.
It removes the need for uncertainty in scientific reports.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two explains how repeated observations improve the orbit estimate.

questions.q: What is the most responsible way to report a newly calculated risk figure?
choices: State whether it is preliminary and explain the uncertainty.
Give the largest number without its context to attract attention.
Present every change as proof that scientists are guessing.
Treat all close approaches as equally dangerous.
questions.explanation: The writer says risk numbers should be accompanied by evidence quality and uncertainty.

questions.q: What does the changing estimate for 2024 YR4 illustrate?
choices: Its size increased rapidly during the observations.
A change in orbit was caused by news reports.
A temporary higher risk estimate can fall after the orbit is refined.
The asteroid's final impact date became more certain each week.
questions.explanation: The example shows that new measurements can strongly reduce an earlier estimated probability.

questions.q: Why was the YR4 sequence unsurprising to astronomers?
choices: Because preliminary orbital probabilities are expected to change with evidence.
Because the original measurements were deliberately misleading.
Because large telescopes always report identical estimates.
Because every asteroid's impact probability must rise first.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three presents updated risk estimates as normal consequences of accumulating data.

questions.q: What is the justified conclusion from the DART collision?
choices: A single spacecraft can destroy any asteroid approaching Earth.
It showed that a spacecraft can alter an orbit, but not that every impact is preventable.
A dangerous asteroid must always have the same structure as Dimorphos.
The tested technique works equally well without advance notice.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four states a demonstrated deflection is not universal protection.

questions.q: Why does the amount of warning time matter to a possible response?
choices: It determines whether a telescope can take photographs.
It proves whether an asteroid will pass through the belt.
It fixes the asteroid's composition in advance.
Changing an orbit takes planning and cannot be treated as instantaneous.
questions.explanation: The text explains that size, structure and available warning time affect the response.

questions.q: What should organisations communicating asteroid risks share?
choices: Only the newest probability without older context.
Predictions only after every uncertainty has disappeared.
Reliable information and explanations of why estimates change.
Dramatic imagery intended to increase interest in emergencies.
questions.explanation: The conclusion advocates cooperative communication that distinguishes knowledge from uncertainty.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the author's overall advice to readers?
choices: Evaluate new claims through evidence, careful preparation and cooperation.
Avoid reading about asteroids until a real threat appears.
Assume that experiments have already made Earth completely safe.
Treat every risk estimate as a permanent fact.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph rejects both panic and complacency in favour of reasoned preparedness.
